items.prompt: A bakery in Otjiwarongo mills its own flour, bakes the bread and sells it over the counter. Explain why one business can appear in more than one sector classification.
items.canonical_answer: The classification follows the stage of the work done to materials. Milling grain is secondary work, because it transforms a raw material; baking is also secondary; selling bread over the counter is a retail service, which belongs to the tertiary sector. The reason one business can appear in more than one classification is that its work spans stages: the flour, the loaf and the sale are different kinds of activity even inside one business. Where a business spans stages, the sector given is the one describing its main stage of activity, which for a bakery is usually secondary.
marking_guidance: Reason: award for the classification following the stage of work, because transforming materials and providing a service are different stages. Second reason: award for the bakery's work spanning stages - milling and baking against retailing - which is why more than one sector can describe it.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the basis on which businesses are classified into the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.
items.canonical_answer: The basis has three features, one per sector. Primary: the work takes materials from the natural world, as in farming, fishing, forestry and mining. Secondary: the work transforms materials into finished goods, through manufacturing or construction. Tertiary: the work provides a service rather than a physical product, as in transport, banking and retailing. What the basis includes is the stage of the work done to materials - taking it, transforming it or serving the customer - and the classification of any business follows that stage rather than the country it operates in or the price of its product.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element of the basis - taking materials from nature, transforming materials into goods, providing services - with one mark for what the classification includes overall: the stage of the work.

items.prompt: A developed economy has introduced automated production lines in most of its factories, and household incomes there have been rising for a decade. Explain how these changes could lead to the tertiary sector becoming the largest sector of that economy.
items.canonical_answer: Condition: the starting points are automated factory lines and rising household incomes. Mechanism: automation lets each factory worker produce far more, so the same output needs fewer factory workers than before, and manufacturing's share of jobs falls; at the same time, rising incomes let households spend a growing share on services such as eating out, insurance and phone data, so service businesses expand. Consequence for the economy: output and employment shift towards services, which leads to the tertiary sector becoming the largest - the outcome the objective of growing national income is usually served by, since services take up the rising spending. For workers as a stakeholder group, the displaced factory workers tend to seek service jobs, reinforcing the same shift.
marking_guidance: Condition: the mechanism must be tied to the given starting points - automation and rising incomes. Mechanism: award for the why or how - fewer workers needed per unit of output, and spending shifting towards services. Consequence: award for the effect on the economy - the tertiary sector becoming the largest - and a second consequence for a stakeholder group, such as factory workers moving into service jobs.

items.prompt: A Ministry of Labour report for a developing economy counts 240 000 workers in farming and fishing, 60 000 in factory work and 300 000 in services. Farm mechanisation is expected to reduce the farming count over the next decade. Explain what the figures suggest about this economy's sector classification, and what is likely to happen to the counts over the decade.
items.canonical_answer: The facts here suggest a developing economy: primary work at 240 000 jobs is still close behind services at 300 000, and both dwarf the 60 000 in factories, which is a shape a developed economy - where primary work is typically a very small share - would not show. The reasoning about the decade: mechanisation reduces the farming count, because machines mean fewer people are needed per hectare, and the displaced workers tend to move towards towns and service work. So the likely pattern is the primary count falling, the services count rising, and the factory count changing little - the same shift towards services that developed economies have already been through. The conclusion for this economy is a rising tertiary share, driven by workers leaving the land rather than by rising incomes alone.
marking_guidance: Context: award for using the business's facts - 240 000 against 60 000 and 300 000 jobs - to identify a developing economy. Reasoning: award for the link between mechanisation and the falling farming count, and the move towards service work. Conclusion: award a choice about the decade that follows the reasoning - the services count rising as primary falls.

items.prompt: Explain the features of the reasons why the importance of business sectors changes between developed and developing economies.
items.canonical_answer: The features of the reasons come in three parts. Income: as households earn more, they spend a growing share on services, so the tertiary share rises - this part is strongest in developed economies, where the tertiary sector tends to be the largest already. Technology: machines and automation let each worker produce far more, so manufacturing needs fewer workers and the secondary share of jobs falls wherever automation spreads. Starting point: in many developing economies most households still depend on farming, fishing and extractive work, so the primary sector employs the most people, and the change begins when mechanisation pushes workers off the land towards towns. What the reasons include overall is movement: the shares shift because people and spending move, not because any single business changes sector.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - rising incomes shifting spending to services, automation shrinking factory jobs, and the primary starting point of developing economies - with one mark for what the reasons include overall: movement of people and spending between sectors.

items.prompt: A learner writes: "A Windhoek studio develops new software products for other businesses, so it is in the secondary sector, because it works on products." Explain why this statement is wrong.
items.canonical_answer: The error is treating any work connected to a product as manufacturing. In fact, making a product - physically transforming materials into finished goods, as a bottling line or a furniture workshop does - is secondary-sector work, whereas developing a product, such as designing and coding software for a customer, transforms no materials: it supplies skill and design work, which is a service belonging to the tertiary sector. The test that tells the ideas apart: ask whether the business physically transforms materials into a finished good (making, secondary) or supplies its thinking and design to a customer (developing, a tertiary service). The distinction matters to changing sector importance: as economies develop, a growing share of product work moves from making to developing, which is one reason the tertiary share tends to rise while the secondary share of jobs falls.
marking_guidance: The error is named and corrected: in fact making a product (physical transformation, secondary) differs from developing a product (design and skill supplied to a customer, a tertiary service). Award the second mark for the test that separates the confused pair - whether materials are physically transformed.

items.prompt: A family-owned fishing company in Walvis Bay and NamWater, the state-owned water utility, both operate in Namibia. Explain the distinction between the private sector and the public sector, using these two businesses.
items.canonical_answer: The boundary is ownership and control by the state. The fishing company belongs to a family, which controls it and runs it for profit: private sector. NamWater belongs to the state, is controlled by government and is run to provide water the population needs rather than to profit: public sector. The distinction shows on both sides: ownership - private owners against the state - and main aim - profit against providing a service. In a mixed economy such as Namibia's, both sectors operate side by side, which is why the two businesses can share a country and differ completely in who owns them and what they are for.
marking_guidance: Boundary: award for naming the dividing line - state ownership and control against private ownership. Both sides: award for applying it to the two named businesses, the family company against the state utility, on ownership and aim.

items.prompt: Explain the features used to classify a business enterprise between the private sector and the public sector.
items.canonical_answer: The features are three. Ownership: a private-sector business is owned by individuals or companies, whereas a public-sector organisation is owned by the state. Main aim: private-sector businesses are usually run for profit, whereas public-sector organisations usually aim to provide a service the population needs. Control: private owners and shareholders direct their own business, whereas government ministers and officials direct the public sector. What the features include is a single test: identify who owns the enterprise, what its main aim is and who controls it, and the sector classification follows - the parts work together rather than separately.
marking_guidance: Features: award for each element - ownership, main aim, control - with one mark for what the classification includes when the parts are used together.

items.prompt: The manager of Oshakati Premier Juice, a private juice processor, is writing a report for a lender about the industry around her business. Fruit growing in the region is moving to mechanical harvesters, and two rival processors have automated their bottling lines. Write several linked points for the manager: state the sector the juice processor sits in and one sector each for its main supplier and its main customer, give a reason for each classification, and state what the changes in the surrounding industry are likely to mean for the counts of workers in each sector.
items.canonical_answer: Oshakati Premier Juice sits in the secondary sector, because its work transforms fruit - a primary product - into bottled juice. Its main supplier, the fruit grower, sits in the primary sector, because the work takes growing materials from the natural world. Its main customer, a supermarket chain, sits in the tertiary sector, because retailing is a service rather than a physical product. The likely effects on worker counts: mechanical harvesters mean fewer workers are needed per orchard, so the primary count around the region tends to fall; automated bottling lines mean the same output needs fewer factory workers, so the secondary count tends to fall too. Each point holds for this business's surroundings - the harvester change bites in the orchards that supply the processor, and the automation change bites in the bottling halls it competes with.
marking_guidance: Point: award for each classification stated - processor secondary, grower primary, customer tertiary. Reason: award for the because behind each - transforming materials, taking from nature, providing a service. Context: award for applying each point to the named business and its surroundings - the harvesters in the supplying orchards and the automation in rival bottling lines.

items.prompt: A government panel is reviewing the economy's sector counts: primary work 240 000 workers, secondary work 60 000 and services 300 000. Incomes have been rising by 4 per cent a year, and the panel expects farm mechanisation to continue. The panel must decide whether to spend its next budget on supporting service businesses or on supporting factories. Using the figures, consider which choice the panel should make.
items.canonical_answer: The figures: services at 300 000 workers are already the largest group, and primary work at 240 000 is far larger than the 60 000 in factories - the shape of a developing economy. Judgement: the panel should direct most of the budget towards service businesses, with a recommendation to monitor the factory group rather than expand it. Context for the judgement: rising incomes of 4 per cent a year let households spend a growing share on services, so service demand is likely to grow on its own; and mechanisation is likely to push workers off the land towards towns, where service work - taxis, security, retail - is where they mainly land, so services will need to absorb the most people. The criterion that decides it is where the moving workers and the rising spending both point: services. Counterargument: the factories group is the smallest, and a supporter of factory spending could argue that secondary work adds more value per worker and that abandoning it risks depending on imports - the panel's figures do not settle that either way. Condition: the recommendation depends on the mechanisation forecast holding; if mechanisation stalls, the primary count stays high and the case for service spending weakens.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on where the budget goes. Context: award for using the figures - 240 000 against 60 000 and 300 000 workers, and the 4 per cent income rise. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - where the moving workers and rising spending point. Counterargument: award for the case against the recommendation, such as value added per factory worker. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on the mechanisation forecast.

items.prompt: Plan, without writing the full answer, a response to this 12-mark task: "A developing economy should aim to move its workers out of primary work as fast as possible." Consider this view. Set out the paragraphs you would write, the judgement you would reach and the criterion that decides it, the case against your judgement, and the conditions the final recommendation would depend on.
items.canonical_answer: Plan. Paragraph 1, define the terms: the classification of sectors - primary, secondary, tertiary - and what a falling primary share means, distinguishing the share of workers from the level of farm output. Paragraph 2, the case for the view: primary work is usually the lowest-paid and mechanisation is pushing workers off the land anyway, so aiming to speed the move could raise incomes and match where the spending of richer households goes - services. Paragraph 3, the case against: the food a country eats and the exports it earns often depend on primary work, and a collapse of farming faster than the service sector can absorb workers risks unemployment in the towns; the facts of a developing economy - most households still depending on the land - cut against forcing the pace. Paragraph 4, judgement: the view holds only where service jobs exist to absorb the movers; the criterion is whether the moves are matched by jobs, not the speed of the move itself. Recommendation conditional on: mechanisation proceeding gradually, service businesses creating enough absorption, and farm output being maintained by the remaining workers.
marking_guidance: Judgement: the plan must state the verdict the answer would reach. Context: the plan must use facts about developing economies - dependence on primary work and the mechanisation pressure. Criterion: the plan must name what decides the verdict - moves matched by jobs. Counterargument: the plan must include the case against the view - food and export dependence and unemployment risk. Condition: the recommendation must depend on stated conditions - gradual mechanisation and job absorption.

items.prompt: Rundu Ferry Services is an unfamiliar business a learner is meeting for the first time: a passenger ferry across the Kavango River, set up three years ago by a retired teacher who owns it outright, charging fares that cover costs with a small surplus, and employing six crew. The town's hospital is the district's largest employer, run by the state. The regional council is considering taking the ferry over into public ownership to keep fares low for commuters. Analyse the situation and recommend what the council should do.
items.canonical_answer: Analysis: the ferry is private sector on all three features - owned by the retired teacher, run for the small surplus the fares leave, controlled by its owner. The hospital is public sector on all three: state-owned, service-aimed, government-controlled. That is the classification the objective asks for, and it is what makes the council's proposal a genuine change of sector, not just a change of management. Consequences to weigh: public ownership would place the fare level under the council, which supports the aim of keeping fares low for commuters; but the ferry's surpluses are what maintain the boats, and the classification change removes the owner's profit motive, which can weaken the incentive to run efficiently - a risk the six crew's jobs rest on. The context facts - a three-year-old business, one owner, six crew - mean the council is absorbing a small operation whose survival currently depends on one person. Recommendation: the council should not take the ferry into public ownership outright; a subsidy per crossing, conditional on the ferry keeping fares at an agreed level, keeps the private owner running the boats while protecting commuters, and depends on the council being able to fund the subsidy and on the owner agreeing to the fare condition.
marking_guidance: Judgement: award for a clear recommendation on the takeover. Context: award for using the facts of the case - owner-operated ferry, small surpluses, six crew, state hospital as the public-sector contrast. Criterion: award for naming what decides it - fare protection against the efficiency risk of removing the profit motive. Counterargument: award for the case against the recommendation, such as the cost of subsidies or the owner refusing. Condition: award for the recommendation depending on stated conditions - funding the subsidy and the owner's agreement.
